top_choice_rationale: P001 (Helpman and Grossman, with the citation confined to the political economy of trade protection) has the cleanest attribution on the slate: a long, tightly coupled two-person programme with no uncredited co-originator at the same level. The protection-for-sale framework turned a qualitative claim, that organised interests bend policy, into an equilibrium model with sharp cross-sector predictions, which made policy influence measurable. It has been tested, criticised and extended for about three decades, so maturity is not in doubt. The main limit is that empirical support for the specific predictions is mixed and specification-sensitive. I treat the contribution as a framework and research programme, not a confirmed quantitative result, and I would not let the citation imply otherwise. I would also keep the growth strand out of the citation, because I cannot verify any overlap with the 2025 prize. P002 (Autor, Dorn and Hanson) is second. It is design-based evidence of high importance, and the set of three names is now stable. It ranks below P001 because the persistence and magnitude of the effects and the shift-share identification are still being re-estimated, and the task-framework antecedents lie outside the credited names. P003 (Melitz and Helpman) is third. Its empirical confrontation is dense, but the omission of Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum is an attribution gap that three names cannot close without weakening the core, and the pivotal contribution rests largely on one 2003 paper. I rank all three above no award because each is a substantive, mature contribution. This ordering rests on the written round-2 files and general knowledge, not on independently verified citation or impact data. It does not count the number of supporters as merit.
recusal_note: none apparent from profile for P001 (Grossman, Helpman), P002 (Autor, Dorn, Hanson) or P003 (Helpman, Melitz). My profile lists no collaboration or institutional tie to any of them. For disclosure only: I am a Stockholm University colleague, in a different department, of committee members Hassler, Krusell and Boppart. My co-authorship with Persson and Rothstein, and the IIES link to Persson, concern B036, which is not on this slate. My field is close to the political-economy side of P001, and I have applied the same criteria across fields. Disclosed, not adjudicated.
